                    ### Question
                    A 37-year-old man presents a picture of arthritis of the metacarpophalangeal of both hands and a right pleuritis. On examination, bilateral malar erythema was observed. Positive antinuclear antibodies are detected (titre 1/640), with native anti-DNA antibodies also positive; Anti-Sm negative. What would be the initial treatment of choice for this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Glucocorticoids at high doses.
opb. Glucocorticoids and mycophenolate.
opc. Non-steroidal and antimalarial anti-inflammatories.
opd. The picture will probably be self-limiting and does not require treatment.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of arthritis, pleuritis, bilateral malar erythema, and positive antinuclear and anti-DNA antibodies strongly suggests a diagnosis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). Standard medical consensus for initial treatment of SLE, particularly with mild to moderate symptoms such as arthritis and skin manifestations, includes the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for joint pain and antimalarials (such as hydroxychloroquine) for skin and systemic symptoms. The retrieved evidence paths support the association of SLE with antinuclear and anti-DNA antibodies, confirming the diagnosis. High-dose glucocorticoids or immunosuppressants like mycophenolate are typically reserved for more severe manifestations of SLE, such as significant organ involvement, which is not indicated in this case. Therefore, the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient is the combination of NSAIDs and antimalarials.
